parole.testo: From New Latin euphoria, from Ancient Greek εὐφορίᾱ (euphoríā), from εὔφορος (eúphoros, “bearing well”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear”).
Internationalism. Through European languages, from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

Internationalism. From אָטוֹם (“an atom”) + ־י (-í, “-ic, -ish, -like”), through European languages, from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).
Attested since Mishnaic Hebrew, from Latin ītalicus or Ancient Greek ἰταλικός (italikós).

Ultimately from New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”), from ἀνά (aná, “up against”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “spending time”), which from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).
Learned borrowing from Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).

Internationalism. Borrowed from New Latin encyclopaedīa and its borrowings in European languages; ultimately from a false univerbated form of Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular”) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā, “education”, literally “rearing of a child”).
From Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía).

From Latin byzantinus, from Ancient Greek Βυζάντιον (Buzántion, “Byzantium”).
Ultimately from Latin galaxias, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “Milky Way”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).
Borrowed from Latin diplōma, from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “folded paper, license”). Compare דִּיפְּלוֹמָט (diplómat, “a diplomat”).

parole.significato: curtain (piece of cloth covering a window)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin vēlum, likely through Ancient Greek βῆλον (bêlon).
Internationalism from Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + -metria (“-metry”).
Ultimately from Latin chīrūrgia, from chīrurgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós). Cognate with Russian хирургия (xirurgija), Polish chirurgia and other Slavic synonyms.
Ultimately from Latin meteōrum, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron).

parole.significato: mythology, the collection of myths concerning a people, culture, or nation
parole.testo: From Latin mythologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”).

Ultimately borrowed from Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, study, learning”). Reinforced by English mathematics and its cognates.

parole.significato: dagger (a stabbing weapon, similar to a sword but with a short, double-edged blade)
parole.testo: From Latin pugiō, pūgiōnem, perhaps via Ancient Greek φουγίων (phougíōn).

Ultimately from Latin pyrotechnica, from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + τεχνικός (tekhnikós, “skillful, workmanlike”).
From European languages, such as English plastic.

parole.significato: psychology (the study of the human mind)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Renaissance Latin psychologia (coined by Marko Marulić from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “study of”)). Cognate with Russian психология (psixologija), Polish psychologia and other Slavic synonyms.
Ultimately borrowed from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”).
Internationalism, derived from Latin parodia and Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía).

parole.significato: a quill, reed pen, or metal dip pen
parole.testo: From Latin culmus or Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed”), compare Arabic قَلَم (qalam).
Via various European languages from Latin (ecclesia) cathedralis, from cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).
